'''Richard William Carthew''' (born 5 September 1956) is a [[Developmental biology|developmental biologist]] and [[Quantitative biology|quantitative biologist]] at Northwestern University. He is a professor of molecular biosciences and is the director of the NSF-Simons Center for Quantitative Biology.

== Education and early career ==
Carthew received his B.Sc. degree in biology from [[Queen's University at Kingston|Queen's University]] in 1978. There, he pursued his interests in ecology by conducting research under the supervision of Ted Brown<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Smol|first=John P.|date=December 1986|title=A biographical sketch of Seward R. (Ted) Brown|journal=Hydrobiologia|volume=143|issue=1|pages=9–11|doi=10.1007/BF00026638|bibcode=1986HyBio.143....9S |s2cid=36992974|issn=0018-8158}}</ref> on the environmental adaptation of cyanobacteria. Carthew continued his studies at [[University of Toronto]], where he received a M.Sc. degree in botany with Johann Hellebust. concurrently, he undertook training in music composition at the Royal Conservatory of Music in Toronto.

Upon completing of his degree, Carthew worked for two years as a research technician under the supervision of [[Jack Greenblatt]] at the Banting and Best Department of Medical Research in Toronto. During this time, he studied the biochemistry of [[Eukaryote|eukaryotic]] gene transcription and decided to forgo a career in music for one in the biomedical sciences. In 1982, Carthew began his PhD studies at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] where he conducted his thesis research in the lab of [[Phillip Allen Sharp|Phillip A. Sharp]]. During his doctoral studies, Carthew transformed the Electrophoresis Mobility Shift Assay (EMSA) into an assay capable of detecting sequence-specific DNA-binding proteins from crude cell extracts.<ref name="Carthew 439–448">{{Cite journal|last1=Carthew|first1=Richard W.|last2=Chodosh|first2=Lewis A.|last3=Sharp|first3=Phillip A.|date=December 1985|title=An RNA polymerase II transcription factor binds to an upstream element in the adenovirus major late promoter|journal=Cell|volume=43|issue=2|pages=439–448|doi=10.1016/0092-8674(85)90174-6|pmid=4075400|issn=0092-8674|doi-access=free}}</ref> Using this method, he identified and studied the HeLa cell transcription factor [[USF1|USF]] and its role in regulating gene transcription.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Chodosh|first1=L A|last2=Carthew|first2=R W|last3=Sharp|first3=P A|date=December 1986|title=A single polypeptide possesses the binding and transcription activities of the adenovirus major late transcription factor.|journal=Molecular and Cellular Biology|volume=6|issue=12|pages=4723–4733|doi=10.1128/mcb.6.12.4723|pmid=3796614|pmc=367258|issn=0270-7306|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Carthew|first1=R W|last2=Chodosh|first2=L A|last3=Sharp|first3=P A|date=1987-11-01|title=The major late transcription factor binds to and activates the mouse metallothionein I promoter.|journal=Genes & Development|volume=1|issue=9|pages=973–980|doi=10.1101/gad.1.9.973|pmid=3428603|issn=0890-9369|doi-access=free}}</ref> Carthew also played a role in popularizing the now-common use in the biomedical literature of having multiple authors of a paper as "co-first authors". Carthew and fellow graduate student Lewis Chodosh decided to adopt this mechanism for their joint publication<ref name="Carthew 439–448"/> in Cell, inspired by its use by [[Andrew Fire]] and Mark Samuels.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Samuels|first1=Mark|last2=Fire|first2=Andrew|date=1982|title=Separation and characterization of factors mediating accurate transcription by RNA polymerase II|journal=Journal of Biological Chemistry|volume=257|issue=23|pages=14419–14427|doi=10.1016/S0021-9258(19)45397-0|pmid=7142220|doi-access=free}}</ref> This novel feature of their paper was noticed by many, and subsequently adopted in other papers.

Following his graduate work, Carthew pursued post-doctoral research at the [[University of California, Berkeley|University of California Berkeley]] as a Helen Hay Whitney fellow. Carthew worked under the direction of [[Gerald M. Rubin]] on the molecular mechanisms of compound eye development in ''[[Drosophila melanogaster]]''. He showed that the [[RING finger domain]] protein [https://www.wikigenes.org/e/gene/e/39884.html Seven in Absentia] is essential for multipotent eye cells to adopt an R7 photoreceptor cell fate.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Carthew|first1=Richard W.|last2=Rubin|first2=Gerald M.|date=November 1990|title=seven in absentia, a gene required for specification of R7 cell fate in the Drosophila eye|journal=Cell|volume=63|issue=3|pages=561–577|doi=10.1016/0092-8674(90)90452-k|pmid=2146028|s2cid=1049619|issn=0092-8674}}</ref> In subsequent work, he showed that Seven in Absentia is activated by the [[Ras GTPase|Ras]] signal transduction pathway and acts as an [[Ubiquitin ligase|E3 ubiquitin ligase]] to rapidly degrade a transcriptional repressor of R7 cell differentiation.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Kauffmann|first1=R C|last2=Li|first2=S|last3=Gallagher|first3=P A|last4=Zhang|first4=J|last5=Carthew|first5=R W|date=1996-09-01|title=Ras1 signaling and transcriptional competence in the R7 cell of Drosophila.|journal=Genes & Development|volume=10|issue=17|pages=2167–2178|doi=10.1101/gad.10.17.2167|pmid=8804311|issn=0890-9369|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Li|first1=Songhui|last2=Li|first2=Ying|last3=Carthew|first3=Richard W|last4=Lai|first4=Zhi-Chun|date=August 1997|title=Photoreceptor Cell Differentiation Requires Regulated Proteolysis of the Transcriptional Repressor Tramtrack|journal=Cell|volume=90|issue=3|pages=469–478|doi=10.1016/s0092-8674(00)80507-3|pmid=9267027|s2cid=7853369|issn=0092-8674|doi-access=free}}</ref>

== Faculty career ==
Carthew started his independent research group in 1992 at the [[University of Pittsburgh]] in the Department of Biological Sciences. He became a tenured associate professor in 1998 and full professor in 2001. In 2001, Carthew moved to [[Northwestern University]] and became a full professor in the Department of Molecular Biosciences, which is located on the Evanston campus. He was appointed the Owen L. Coon Professor of Molecular Biology in 2006. Carthew served as leader of the Chromatin and Nuclear Dynamics Program in Northwestern’s Robert H. Lurie Comprehensive Cancer Center from 2012 to 2018. He served as director of the NCI funded Oncogenesis and Developmental Biology Training Program from 2007 to 2014. He currently serves as director of the NIGMS funded Training Program in Cellular and Molecular Basis of Disease at Northwestern.

In the early phase of Carthew lab research, a number of firsts were achieved. The Carthew group was the first to establish the ''Drosophila'' eye as a model system to study planar cell polarity.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Zheng|first1=L|last2=Zhang|first2=J.|last3=Carthew|first3=R.W.|date=1995|title=frizzled regulates mirror-symmetric pattern formation in the Drosophila eye|url=https://dev.biologists.org/content/121/9/3045.long|journal=Development|volume=121|issue=9|pages=3045–3055|doi=10.1242/dev.121.9.3045|pmid=7555730|url-access=subscription}}</ref> It was the first group to use ''Drosophila'' as a disease model to screen and test small molecule drugs for potential efficacy in disease treatment.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Kauffmann|first1=R. C.|last2=Qian|first2=Y.|last3=Vogt|first3=A.|last4=Sebti|first4=S. M.|last5=Hamilton|first5=A. D.|last6=Carthew|first6=R. W.|date=1995-11-21|title=Activated Drosophila Ras1 is selectively suppressed by isoprenyl transferase inhibitors.|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|volume=92|issue=24|pages=10919–10923|doi=10.1073/pnas.92.24.10919|pmid=7479910|pmc=40542|issn=0027-8424|bibcode=1995PNAS...9210919K|doi-access=free}}</ref> It was the first group to provide genetic evidence that [[Frizzled]] proteins were [[Wnt signaling pathway|Wnt]] receptors in vivo.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Zhang|first1=J.|last2=Carthew|first2=R. W.|date=1998-08-15|title=Interactions between Wingless and DFz2 during Drosophila wing development|url=https://dev.biologists.org/content/125/16/3075|journal=Development|volume=125|issue=16|pages=3075–3085|doi=10.1242/dev.125.16.3075|issn=0950-1991|pmid=9671581|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last1=Kennerdell|first1=Jason R|last2=Carthew|first2=Richard W|date=December 1998|title=Use of dsRNA-Mediated Genetic Interference to Demonstrate that frizzled and frizzled 2 Act in the Wingless Pathway|journal=Cell|volume=95|issue=7|pages=1017–1026|doi=10.1016/s0092-8674(00)81725-0|pmid=9875855|s2cid=18443540|issn=0092-8674|doi-access=free}}</ref> In 1998, the group discovered that ''Drosophila'' were capable of RNAi or [[RNA interference]].<ref name=":0" /> The labs of [[Andrew Fire]] and [[Craig Mello]] had just demonstrated a key role for double-stranded RNA as the trigger for RNAi in the nematode ''Caenorhabditis elegans'',<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Fire|first1=Andrew|last2=Xu|first2=SiQun|last3=Montgomery|first3=Mary K.|last4=Kostas|first4=Steven A.|last5=Driver|first5=Samuel E.|last6=Mello|first6=Craig C.|date=February 1998|title=Potent and specific genetic interference by double-stranded RNA in Caenorhabditis elegans|journal=Nature|volume=391|issue=6669|pages=806–811|doi=10.1038/35888|pmid=9486653|issn=1476-4687|bibcode=1998Natur.391..806F|s2cid=4355692|url=http://www.dspace.cam.ac.uk/handle/1810/238264 }}</ref> a discovery culminating in a [[Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine|Nobel Prize]] for Fire and Mello in 2006. By showing that RNAi also existed in another animal species, the Carthew group stimulated the search for RNAi in mammals, as well as the adoption of ''Drosophila'' as a premier model to study the biochemical and genetic mechanisms of RNAi. The Carthew group also developed the first and second generations of [[transgene]] systems for performing RNAi against any ''Drosophila'' gene at any stage of the life cycle in a tissue- or cell-specific manner.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Kennerdell|first1=Jason R.|last2=Carthew|first2=Richard W.|date=August 2000|title=Heritable gene silencing in Drosophila using double-stranded RNA|journal=Nature Biotechnology|volume=18|issue=8|pages=896–898|doi=10.1038/78531|pmid=10932163|s2cid=22987734|issn=1087-0156}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Sik Lee|first1=Young|last2=Carthew|first2=Richard W.|date=2003-08-01|title=Making a better RNAi vector for Drosophila: use of intron spacers|journal=Methods|series=RNA interference|volume=30|issue=4|pages=322–329|doi=10.1016/S1046-2023(03)00051-3|pmid=12828946|issn=1046-2023}}</ref> The second generation system was later expanded into a genome-wide collection of transgenic lines targeting all annotated genes.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Dietzl|first1=Georg|last2=Chen|first2=Doris|last3=Schnorrer|first3=Frank|last4=Su|first4=Kuan-Chung|last5=Barinova|first5=Yulia|last6=Fellner|first6=Michaela|last7=Gasser|first7=Beate|last8=Kinsey|first8=Kaolin|last9=Oppel|first9=Silvia|last10=Scheiblauer|first10=Susanne|last11=Couto|first11=Africa|date=July 2007|title=A genome-wide transgenic RNAi library for conditional gene inactivation in Drosophila|journal=Nature|volume=448|issue=7150|pages=151–156|doi=10.1038/nature05954|pmid=17625558|issn=1476-4687|bibcode=2007Natur.448..151D|s2cid=4392409}}</ref> The Carthew lab has continued pursuing the mechanisms and functions of the small non-coding RNA world that was first glimpsed through the lens of RNAi. The group has been addressing how and why [[small interfering RNA]]s (siRNAs) and [[microRNA]]s (miRNAs) regulate gene expression.

Since 2004, the Carthew group has also pursued questions related to quantitative issues of development. Inspired by the mathematical biologist [[D'Arcy Wentworth Thompson|D'Arcy Thompson]] and his seminal book [[On Growth and Form]], the group showed that the topology of epithelial cells in the ''Drosophila'' eye is constrained due to a tendency for the cells to minimize surface energy.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Hayashi|first1=Takashi|last2=Carthew|first2=Richard W.|date=October 2004|title=Surface mechanics mediate pattern formation in the developing retina|journal=Nature|volume=431|issue=7009|pages=647–652|doi=10.1038/nature02952|pmid=15470418|issn=0028-0836|bibcode=2004Natur.431..647H|s2cid=4340509}}</ref> This pioneering work emerged at the same time as other groups around the world also began addressing physical aspects of morphogenesis. Recent work in the Carthew lab has turned to dynamical features of gene expression as cells undergo lineage restriction during development.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Peláez|first1=Nicolás|last2=Gavalda-Miralles|first2=Arnau|last3=Wang|first3=Bao|last4=Navarro|first4=Heliodoro Tejedor|last5=Gudjonson|first5=Herman|last6=Rebay|first6=Ilaria|last7=Dinner|first7=Aaron R|author8-link=Aggelos Katsaggelos|last8=Katsaggelos|first8=Aggelos K|last9=Amaral|first9=Luís AN|last10=Carthew|first10=Richard W|title=Dynamics and heterogeneity of a fate determinant during transition towards cell differentiation|journal=eLife|volume=4|doi=10.7554/eLife.08924|issn=2050-084X|pmc=4720516|pmid=26583752|year=2015 |doi-access=free }}</ref> This work has focused on the importance of time as a dimension in animal development and how [[gene regulatory network]]s are designed to provide temporal flexibility to development. The Carthew group found that when developmental tempo is slowed down by limiting cell metabolism, gene repressors become redundant during lineage restriction, and the entire microRNA family is rendered non-essential for development in general.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Repressive gene regulation synchronizes development with cellular metabolism|last=Cassidy, Justin J. Bernasek, Sebastian M. Bakker, Rachael Giri, Ritika Peláez, Nicolás Eder, Bryan Bobrowska, Anna Bagheri, Neda Nunes Amaral, Luis A. Carthew, Richard W.|journal=Cell|date=2019-07-25|volume=178|issue=4|pages=980–992.e17|publisher=Elsevier|doi=10.1016/j.cell.2019.06.023|pmid=31353220|pmc=6865806|oclc=1111530678}}</ref>

== NSF-Simons Center for Quantitative Biology ==
In July 2018, Carthew became Director of the newly founded NSF-Simons Center for Quantitative Biology at Northwestern University. Co-funded by a public-private partnership between the [[National Science Foundation]] and [[Simons Foundation]], the Center for Quantitative Biology contains 12 Northwestern faculty members who are experts in developmental biology, applied mathematics, and pure mathematics. The Center's mission is to greatly expand the application of mathematics to study of important questions in developmental biology. This is done by supporting interdisciplinary research within the Center and stimulating interdisciplinary research and training activities across the United States. These efforts are augmented by the efforts of three other NSF-Simons Centers located across the country.
